attempts.raw_response: The combination of extreme aridity and fierce winds created an explosive environment. When ignition finally occurred, the fire spread with terrifying speed across the parched landscape. Trees, shrubs, and underbrush had dried out completely, turning into highly flammable tinder that caught sparks easily. The Santa Ana winds fanned the flames, pushing them forward in a relentless surge that outpaced any reasonable attempt at containment. Embers were thrown miles ahead of the main front, starting new blazes that further expanded the inferno’s reach. Within hours, vast tracts of forest were consumed by roaring tongues of orange and red light. The heat was intense enough to melt glass and warp metal structures. Residents watched in horror as their homes and livelihoods vanished into smoke and ash. The sheer scale of destruction left entire communities devastated, with little hope of recovery amidst the charred remains of what had once been thriving ecosystems and settlements alike.

Overview
In addition to the Santiago Canyon Fire, there were several other significant fires fanned by the same gale force Santa Ana winds in San Diego and San Bernardino counties. The Santiago Canyon Fire was the largest and has been estimated as being greater than . Another wildfire in San Diego County at the time has been estimated to have been greater than . The Orange County fire burned through areas of chaparral and coastal sage scrub, as well as a number of farm fields in the Santa Ana Valley, where farmers attempted to control the fire by plowing ahead of it.
